ACT I — UNDERSTANDING
The Neuroscience of Replacement Behavior
Why Behaviors Don't Stop With Punishment
When your child experiences a trigger — frustration, overwhelm, an unmet want — the amygdala fires first. It's faster than thinking. Before the prefrontal cortex (the planning brain) can intervene, the behavior happens. Consequences and punishment try to work after the behavior. But the behavior was already automatic.
What Replacement Behavior Training Does
It installs a faster route. Through repeated practice, a new neural pathway forms: Trigger → reach for the card / use the words / tap the board → need met. Over weeks of consistent practice, this new route becomes the automatic one.
This is neuroplasticity in action. The child's brain literally rewires. The old pathway weakens. The new pathway strengthens — not because of punishment, but because of skill.
Source: Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020); Carr & Durand (1985, JABA)

ACT II — KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER
Building Replacement Behaviors
A.K.A. "Teach Instead of Stop" | Functional Communication Training | FCT

Formal Name: Replacement Behavior Training / Functional Communication Training (FCT) / Functionally Equivalent Alternative Behavior Teaching / Differential Reinforcement of Alternative Behavior (DRA)
Parent-Friendly Definition
Replacement behavior training is the science of teaching your child a better tool for the same job. Every challenging behavior — hitting, screaming, running, grabbing — is currently working for your child. The solution isn't to take away their tool without giving them a better one. The solution is to teach a new behavior that:
Same Need
Meets the same need as the problem behavior
Easier & Faster
Is easier and faster to use than the problem behavior
Works Reliably
Works every single time it's used
Socially Accepted
Acceptable in home, school, and community
Domain: Behavior Support
Age: 2–10 years
10–20 min sessions
3–5× per week

ACT II — DISCIPLINES
The Consortium Behind This Technique
ABA / BCBA (Primary Lead)
Board Certified Behavior Analysts conduct the Functional Behavior Assessment (FBA) to identify why the behavior occurs, then design the replacement behavior protocol. BCBAs determine the reinforcement schedule and monitor data.
Speech-Language Pathologist (SLP)
SLPs lead the communication replacement component — selecting the right alternative communication system (PECS, AAC, vocal training, sign language) matched to the child's current language level.
Occupational Therapist (OT)
OTs address sensory-driven behaviors, designing sensory-based replacement behaviors (proprioceptive input tools, sensory breaks, fidget tools) that meet the same sensory need acceptably.
Special Educator (SpEd)
Special educators implement replacement behaviors in structured learning environments and ensure school-home consistency in the behavior support plan.
NeuroDev Pediatrician
NeuroDev doctors assess for underlying medical contributors (pain, GI issues, sleep disorders, medication effects) and ensure the behavioral intervention is not masking a treatable medical condition.
"The brain does not organize by therapy type. A child who hits during homework may be acting from sensory overwhelm, communication failure, frustration with task demand, reinforcement history, and sleep deprivation — simultaneously." — Pinnacle Blooms Consortium

ACT II — TARGETS
Precision Targets: What Replacement Behavior Training Addresses
🎯 Primary Targets
  • Hitting, biting, scratching (aggression)
  • Screaming, crying as primary communication
  • Running away / elopement
  • Throwing objects / property destruction

  • Emotional identification and labeling

ACT II — SAFETY
Before You Begin: Safety Gate
🔴 RED — Do NOT Proceed If:
  • The challenging behavior involves self-injury → Call 9100 181 181 first
  • Child has displayed behavior endangering safety of others → Requires BCBA-guided Behavior Intervention Plan
  • Child is currently experiencing a medical event, illness, or significant sleep disruption → Postpone
  • You are attempting complete extinction without professional guidance → Extinction causes response bursts that can be dangerous
🟡 AMBER — Proceed With Modification If:
  • Child is overtired or hungry → Shorten to a single practice trial; prioritize basic needs first
  • Child had a difficult day → Use the simplified version; offer the replacement behavior prompt once, end positively
  • Materials not yet available → Use DIY alternatives from Card 10; never delay waiting for perfect materials
🟢 GREEN — Safe to Proceed When:
  • Child is fed, rested, in a baseline regulated state
  • You have your replacement behavior material ready (even DIY)
  • You are calm — your nervous system regulation is the foundation of every session
  • The environment is prepared (see Card 12)

🛑 Stop immediately and seek help if: Any self-injurious behavior that breaks skin or causes bruising · Escalating aggression that endangers anyone's physical safety · Dissociative or unresponsive states · Regression in a previously mastered skill accompanied by physical symptoms.
Immediate contact: 9100 181 181 | care@pinnacleblooms.org
ACT II — SETUP
The Physical Stage: Setting Up for Success
✅ Remove or Minimize
  • Television, tablets, loud music (competing for attention)
  • Other children in the session space
  • High-preference items not being used in the session
✅ Prepare
  • Replacement behavior materials at hand (cards, board, token system)
  • Reinforcement items identified and ready (small, immediately deliverable)
  • Timer visible to child (visual timer preferred)
  • Your calm-down tool within reach
  • "All done" signal ready (visual or verbal cue for session end)
✅ Environment
  • Lighting: Warm, not harsh fluorescent
  • Sound: Quiet or soft familiar background music
  • Temperature: Comfortable — overheating increases dysregulation
  • Space: Enough for the child to move without knocking materials

STEP 1 OF 6
Step 1: Understand the Function — Then Invite the Practice
◉ Step 1 of 6 | Timing: 2–3 minutes

Before introducing any replacement behavior material, you need to know: Why does this behavior happen for my child?
The 4 Functions of Behavior (BACB Framework)
Function
Your Child Behaves To...
The Replacement Teaches...
ATTENTION
Get social response (positive or negative)
A better way to get attention (tap + "excuse me," look-at-me card)
ESCAPE
Get away from demands, people, situations
A better way to escape (break card, help card)
TANGIBLE
Get a preferred item or activity
A better way to request (communication card, choice board)
SENSORY
Get or remove sensory input
A sensory substitute (fidget tool, scheduled sensory break)
The Invitation Scripts
For Communication Cards
"Look what I have! Let's try something new today." (Hold card at child's eye level. Smile. No demand language yet.)
For Break Cards
"I'm going to show you a special card. When you need a break, you can use this." (During a calm moment — not during a challenging one.)
For Token Boards
"We're going to play a game today. Every time you [do the replacement behavior], you earn a star. Look!" (Show the reward first.)
STEP 2 OF 6
Step 2: Teach the Exchange — One Trial at a Time
◉ Step 2 of 6 | Timing: 3–5 minutes
The replacement behavior is taught through a direct teaching trial. The four parts work together as a seamless sequence — each step sets up the next.
Set Up the Trigger (controlled)
Create a small, manageable version of the situation where the problem behavior typically occurs. If child hits when frustrated: give a slightly challenging task. If child screams for food: set out a preferred food just out of reach.
Prompt the Replacement Behavior
Immediately — before the behavior escalates — physically guide or gesture toward the replacement. Hand-over-hand: Guide the child's hand to pick up the communication card. Point: Point to the break card on the table.
Honor the Request Immediately
The moment the child uses (even partially uses) the replacement: immediately give what they asked for. Speed matters. Within 3 seconds. No lecture. Just give it.
Pair with Specific Verbal Praise
"Yes! You used your card. Here's your snack." / "You showed me the break card. Great. Let's take a break." / "You asked for help. I love that. Here I am."
🟢 Engagement
Child uses replacement independently or with minimal prompt → Full reinforcement, celebrate
🟡 Tolerance
Child allows physical prompt → Provide reinforcement, reduce prompt level next trial
🔴 Avoidance
Child refuses, moves away → Pause, re-invite gently, or postpone
STEP 3 OF 6 — MATERIAL 1 & 2
Step 3: The Therapeutic Action — Communication Cards & Break Cards
◉ Step 3 of 6 | Timing: 5–10 minutes | All 9 materials share one active ingredient: they give the child a behavior that serves the same function as the problem behavior, but is socially acceptable.
🗂️ Material 1: Communication Cards & PECS Systems
Function: Tangible (requesting items/activities) + Attention
  • WHAT: Child physically exchanges a picture for the requested item or action
  • WHY: Most challenging behavior is unmet communication. Cards provide a low-barrier, reliable way to communicate without words
  • WHERE: Kitchen (food requests), play area (toy requests), wherever requesting currently produces challenging behavior
  • WHEN: At the first sign of wanting — before the behavior escalates
  • HOW: Child picks up picture card → hands it to adult → adult immediately provides the requested item. No delay. No lecture. Pure exchange.

Clinical Insight: PECS Phase I teaches the physical exchange. Even if the child cannot point or gesture, hand-over-hand prompting works. Over 6–8 trials, reduce physical prompt.
🗂️ Material 2: Break Request Cards
Function: Escape (from demands, overwhelm, sensory overload)
  • WHAT: A simple card the child hands to signal "I need a pause from what's happening"
  • WHY: Running away, aggression during tasks, tantrums at demand — these are escape-motivated. The break card gives an acceptable escape route
  • WHERE: Homework area, therapy table, dinner table — wherever demands cause escape behavior
  • WHEN: Teach during calm. Use at first sign of escalation — before the behavior
  • HOW: Child hands break card → adult immediately says "Yes, 2-minute break. Go to your calm spot." → timer set → child returns to task

Clinical Insight: The break MUST work every time during teaching. Honor 100% of break requests during the first 2–4 weeks. If the card doesn't reliably produce a break, the child will return to the behavior that always worked.
STEP 3 OF 6 — MATERIAL 3 & 4
Step 3: Help Request Cards & Emotion Identification Cards
🗂️ Material 3: Help Request Cards
Function: Escape from task difficulty + Attention (assistance)
  • WHAT: A "Help me" card the child uses when a task exceeds current ability
  • WHY: Throwing puzzles, screaming at homework, giving up through aggression — these are frustration behaviors. The help card gives a dignified way to ask
  • WHERE: Any task area where frustration-driven behavior occurs
  • HOW: Child hands help card → adult immediately provides assistance → praise the asking, not just the task completion

Clinical Insight (SpEd): Model using help yourself. "Look, I need help with this! I'll ask for help." Normalizing help-seeking reduces the stigma that keeps some children from using the card.
🗂️ Material 4: Emotion Identification Cards & Feeling Charts
Function: All functions — emotion awareness precedes all regulation
  • WHAT: Picture cards or posted charts showing emotion faces (happy, sad, angry, frustrated, scared, overwhelmed, calm)
  • WHY: Unnamed emotions explode into behavior. Labeled emotions can be managed. This is the prerequisite to all coping skill use
  • WHERE: Every room of the house — kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, living area
  • HOW: "Your face looks frustrated. Show me on the chart — which one?" → child points → "Yes, you're frustrated. What can we do?"

Clinical Insight (NeuroDev): Some children cannot identify emotions from faces (alexithymia is common in autism). Use body sensation prompts: "Your hands are in fists. That's what frustrated feels like in your body."
STEP 3 OF 6 — MATERIAL 5 & 6
Step 3: Coping Strategy Cards & Social Scripts
🗂️ Material 5: Coping Strategy Cards & Calm-Down Menus
Function: Emotional regulation replacement for reactive behavior
  • WHAT: A visual menu of 3–5 specific strategies: deep breaths, squeeze a stress ball, take a break, ask for help, count to 10
  • WHY: Without a menu, the child's only option in a flooded moment is the automatic behavior. A visual menu bypasses the need to think during stress
  • WHEN: Teach each strategy DURING CALM TIME through practice and role-play. Deploy during emotional moments
  • HOW: When child begins escalating → point to menu → "Which one do you want to try?" → model the chosen strategy alongside the child

Clinical Insight (OT): Match strategies to sensory profile. Sensory seekers: active strategies (jumping, squeezing). Sensory avoiders: withdrawal strategies (dark quiet corner, headphones). One size does not fit all.
🗂️ Material 6: Social Scripts & Interaction Guides
Function: Attention (social interaction) + Tangible (social access)
  • WHAT: Index cards with exact words for social situations — "Can I play?" "My turn please" "Excuse me" "I don't like that"
  • WHY: Grabbing toys, hitting to get attention, shutting down — these happen because the child doesn't know what to say. Scripts remove the guesswork
  • WHERE: Everywhere social interaction occurs — home, playground, classroom, therapy
  • HOW: Child reads (or you read) the script → child uses the words → situation resolves → heavy reinforcement for the verbal attempt

Clinical Insight (SLP): Scripts must match the child's verbal level. For minimally verbal children, a single word ("help" / "play" / "mine") is a complete script. Do not require full sentences before the script is "ready to use."
🏛️ Pinnacle Blooms Network® | 70+ Centers | 20M+ Sessions | 97%+ Improvement
STEP 3 OF 6 — MATERIAL 7 & 8
Step 3: Token Boards & Visual Choice Boards
🗂️ Material 7: Token Boards & Reinforcement Systems
Function: All functions — reinforcement makes replacement behaviors worth using
  • WHAT: A visual board where the child earns tokens (stars, stickers, chips) toward a preferred reward
  • WHY: New replacement behaviors need to be MORE reinforcing than the problem behavior. Token boards make the payoff visible, immediate, and predictable
  • WHEN: Every time the replacement behavior occurs (at least during the first 2–4 weeks)
  • HOW: Child uses replacement behavior → immediately give token → pair with specific verbal praise → when board is full → child accesses the reward
🛒 Rosette Imprint Reward Jar — ₹589 → Amazon.in
🛒 1800+ Reward Stickers — ₹364 → Amazon.in

Clinical Insight (BCBA): The most common token board mistake is making it too long (10 tokens before reward). Start with 3 tokens. Quick success → quick reward → child is motivated to try again.
🗂️ Material 8: Visual Choice Boards for Requesting
Function: Tangible (requesting preferred items/activities)
  • WHAT: A board displaying 3–6 pictures of available choices — food items, toys, activities
  • WHY: Grabbing, screaming, tantrums around transitions happen because the child cannot communicate their preference
  • WHEN: Before a transition or demand where problem behavior typically occurs. Offer the choice board proactively — don't wait for the behavior
  • HOW: Show the board → "Which one do you want?" → child points → immediately provide chosen item → reinforce the pointing/selection
STEP 3 OF 6 — MATERIAL 9
Step 3: Self-Monitoring Charts & Tracking Tools
🗂️ Material 9: Self-Monitoring Charts & Behavior Tracking Tools
Function: All functions — internal control as long-term goal
  • WHAT: A chart where the child (not the parent) records their own use of replacement behaviors — check marks, stickers, tally marks
  • WHY: The long-term goal of all replacement behavior training is self-regulation — the child managing their own behavior without external prompts. Self-monitoring builds the metacognitive bridge
  • WHERE: Anywhere the replacement behavior is being tracked
  • WHEN: Best for children 5+ with some self-awareness. Introduce after the replacement behavior is established — not during initial teaching
  • HOW: After child uses replacement behavior → "You used your words! Put a check on your chart." → celebrate the self-recording → review chart together, set daily goals

Clinical Insight (BCBA + SpEd): Self-monitoring is both a measurement tool AND a teaching tool. The act of recording one's own behavior increases that behavior. Children who monitor their replacement behavior use it more — even when adults aren't watching.
All 9 materials have Level I evidence base through meta-analyses and systematic reviews: PMC11506176 | PMC10955541 | NCAEP 2020 | BACB Practice Guidelines | Carr & Durand (1985)

Variation Options — Build Generalization
Change the trigger slightly — different demand, different location
Change the adult — parent vs. sibling vs. grandparent prompts
Change the time of day — morning vs. afternoon sessions
Change the material format — laminated card vs. digital card vs. verbal prompt

Satiation Indicators — Stop the trial when you see: Child repeating replacement behavior with significant reduction in engagement · Child begins escaping the teaching activity itself · Response latency increasing significantly · Eyes glazing or body drooping.
"3 good trials beat 10 forced trials. Quality of the learning moment matters more than quantity of attempts."
STEP 5 OF 6
Step 5: The Reinforcement Moment — Make the Replacement Behavior Win
◉ Step 5 of 6 | Timing: Continuous during session

⏱️ TIMING RULE: Within 3 seconds. Every time. No exceptions during teaching phase. The replacement behavior must produce its reinforcer faster than the problem behavior ever did. This is how the brain chooses skills over behaviors.
🏆 Natural Reinforcers
Communication card → Immediately get the item · Break card → Immediately get the break · Help card → Immediately get the help. These are the strongest reinforcers.
⭐ Token Economy
Token delivered immediately upon replacement behavior use · "You used your words. Here's your star." · Board completion → access to pre-identified reward. Rosette Jar ₹589 | Stickers ₹364
🗣️ Verbal Praise
Immediate, specific, enthusiastic: "Yes! You asked with your card. That was so smart." NOT "Good job." (too vague). NOT delayed praise 2 minutes later (too late).
🤗 Physical Affection
High-five, fist bump, brief hug — immediately after replacement behavior use. Know your child: some children find physical contact aversive. Observe and adjust.
"Celebrate the attempt, not just the success. A shaky, prompted attempt at the replacement behavior still earns full reinforcement. You are reinforcing the direction of travel, not perfect execution." — Pinnacle BCBA Consortium
STEP 6 OF 6
Step 6: The Cool-Down — No Session Ends Abruptly
◉ Step 6 of 6 | Timing: 2–3 minutes
Warning Signal (2 min before end)
"Two more, then we're all done." Hold up two fingers. Show timer.
Final Reinforcement Trial
One final successful replacement behavior trial → deliver reinforcement enthusiastically. End on success.
Material Put-Away Ritual
Invite the child to participate: "Help me put the cards away." This creates closure and signals transition. Child participation in put-away builds routine.
Cool-Down Activity (1–2 min)
Offer a brief, low-demand preferred activity: a favorite book, a short sensory activity, or a quiet movement break (walking to another room).
Transition to Next Activity
"Great work today! Now we're going to [next activity]." Use a visual schedule card if available.

What to Do If Child Resists Ending: Do NOT extend the session (this reinforces resistance) · DO use visual timer: "When the timer beeps, we're done." · DO offer the cool-down activity as the next enjoyable event · DO acknowledge: "I know you like this. We'll do it again tomorrow."

ACT III — TROUBLESHOOTING
Session Troubleshooting — The Reality Card
Most sessions don't go perfectly. That's not failure. That's data.
"My child refused to touch the replacement behavior material at all."
Why: The material itself may be aversive, or motivation wasn't established yet.
Fix: Pair the material with high-preference items first (put stickers ON the card, let child play with the token board before it becomes a contingency). Introduce during play, not as a teaching activity.
"My child used the card once, then went straight back to hitting."
Why: The replacement behavior isn't yet stronger than the problem behavior.
Fix: Speed up your response to the card. Check your honoring rate — are you honoring 100% of card uses?
"My child kept handing the break card but never returned to the task."
Why: The break is too long, too reinforcing, or the task is too aversive.
Fix: Shorten breaks (use a timer — 2 minutes maximum). Return to a modified, easier version of the task.
"My child's problem behavior actually got WORSE after starting this."
Why: This is an extinction burst — a temporary increase in problem behavior when the behavior stops "working" as reliably. This is a clinical sign that the intervention is working.
Fix: Hold firm. Honor replacement behavior every time. This phase passes — usually within 1–2 weeks. Contact your BCBA if severe: 9100 181 181
"The replacement behavior works at home but nowhere else."
Why: Generalization hasn't been taught — the child has learned to use the card with you, in your kitchen, at 4pm. That's all they've learned so far.
Fix: Systematically teach across settings (different rooms → different people → different times → community). This is a Phase 2 goal — not a failure of Phase 1.
"My child would only use the card when physically prompted — never independently."
Why: The independent use skill hasn't been built yet — this is completely normal in early teaching.
Fix: Continue with prompted trials. Gradually fade from physical → gestural → verbal → independent over weeks. Expected in weeks 1–4.
"I can't tell if we're making progress."
Why: Progress in replacement behavior training is often invisible until it's dramatic. Parents frequently miss small changes.
Fix: Review your data from Card 24. Look for: prompt level decreasing, latency to replacement behavior decreasing, child initiating the card without a trigger.
"Session abandonment is not failure. It is data. Every session that doesn't go as planned teaches you something about your child's learning profile that a perfect session never could." — Pinnacle BCBA Consortium
ACT III — PERSONALIZATION
No Two Children Are Identical: Personalization Protocol
⬅️ EASIER VERSION
  • Single replacement behavior, single context, maximum prompts
  • Shorten to 2–3 trials maximum
  • Use most preferred reinforcer available
  • Accept any approximation of the replacement behavior
⚖️ STANDARD VERSION
  • Protocol as described in Cards 14–23
  • Gradual prompt fading across sessions
  • Variable reinforcement as behavior stabilizes
➡️ HARDER VERSION
  • Introduce delay between replacement behavior and reinforcer (build frustration tolerance)
  • Introduce replacement behavior in new setting or with new adult
  • Add self-monitoring (Material 9)
  • Generalize to community settings
Profile-Based Variations
Child Profile
Modification
Non-verbal / Pre-verbal
PECS and choice boards are primary; break cards and help cards use physical exchange only
Minimally verbal
Single word scripts + cards; fade to verbal-only over months
Sensory seeker
Coping menu must include movement-based strategies; token board tokens should be tactile
Sensory avoider
Quiet, low-sensory session environment; avoid high-enthusiasm praise that feels overwhelming
Age 2–4
Maximize natural environment teaching; fewer structured trials, more in-the-moment prompting
Age 6–10
Self-monitoring becomes primary tool; begin internal control building
Cognitive delays
Longer teaching phase, more repetition, most consistent cue possible
ACT IV — PROGRESS ARC
Weeks 1–2: What Progress Actually Looks Like

Most parents expect the problem behavior to stop immediately. Here is what actually happens in weeks 1–2 — and why it represents real progress.
✅ This IS Progress in Weeks 1–2
  • Child tolerates the replacement behavior material being present
  • Child accepts a physical prompt toward the replacement behavior (even once)
  • Problem behavior frequency unchanged — but you now have a teaching structure
  • You as the parent feel more in control (you have a tool, not just consequences)
  • Child shows curiosity about the token board or reward system
❌ Not Expected Yet in Weeks 1–2
  • Independent use of replacement behavior
  • Significant reduction in problem behavior frequency
  • Generalization to new settings
  • Self-monitoring
"If your child tolerates the break card being on the table without throwing it — that is real progress. Week 1 is about establishing the material as safe. Week 2 is about the first prompted exchange. You are laying the neural groundwork." — Pinnacle BCBA Consortium

ACT IV — RED FLAGS
🚨 Red Flags — Even in Success, Stay Watchful
🔴 1. Self-injurious behavior emerges or intensifies
Head banging, self-biting, scratching to bleeding, hair-pulling — during or after attempts at replacement behavior.
Action: Pause home implementation. Call 9100 181 181 immediately. SIB requires professional BCBA assessment.
🔴 2. Aggression escalates significantly (dangerous to others)
Hitting causing injury, biting causing breaks in skin, throwing objects that endanger others. The extinction burst may be unmanageable without behavioral support.
Action: Contact Pinnacle or nearest behavior specialist. Do not attempt extinction without professional support.
🟡 3. Replacement works in teaching setting but problem behavior intensifies everywhere else
Skill is not generalizing; the child is context-discriminating.
Action: Contact child's school to implement replacement behavior protocol there. Request school-home consistency plan.
🟡 4. Child begins using replacement behavior manipulatively
Break card used excessively as avoidance, not genuine need — the break has become the preferred behavior, replacing all tasks.
Action: Implement break card criteria (only during task, limited to 2 breaks per session). Consult BCBA.
🟡 5. Significant regression in a previously mastered skill
Child loses speech, loses toilet training, loses compliance previously present. May indicate medical, environmental, or traumatic stressor.
Action: Medical consultation with NeuroDev pediatrician. Call 9100 181 181.
🟡 6. Caregiver burnout affecting implementation consistency
Parent unable to implement consistently due to emotional exhaustion. Inconsistent implementation extends the learning timeline and can worsen behavior.
Action: Reach out to Pinnacle parent support community. Your wellbeing is a clinical variable.

ACT VI — FAQ · CTA · PROMISE
Your Questions, Answered by the Pinnacle Consortium
How long before I see the problem behavior decrease?
In the first 2–4 weeks, expect replacement behavior acquisition — the child learning the new tool. Problem behavior reduction typically begins in weeks 3–6. Significant reduction (50–70%) occurs by weeks 6–8 with consistent honoring. If no change by week 6, contact your BCBA — the function may not have been correctly identified.
My child doesn't seem motivated by any reward. How do I build a token system?
Every child has reinforcers — they're just not always obvious. Watch what your child seeks, grabs for, or protests losing. Try: edible reinforcers (small pieces of preferred food), access to a preferred screen for 30 seconds, proprioceptive input (crash cushion, trampoline bounce). Reach out to our BCBA team: 9100 181 181
Should I still use consequences for the problem behavior while teaching the replacement?
The most effective approach is DRA: heavy reinforcement for the replacement behavior + minimal response to the problem behavior (not punishment, not excessive attention). Complete extinction should only be implemented under BCBA guidance, as it causes extinction bursts. For safety-related behaviors, call 9100 181 181.
My child can talk. Do they still need cards?
Yes — initially. Cards reduce the cognitive demand of producing language under stress. A verbal child who hits when frustrated may know the words "I'm frustrated" but cannot access them during emotional flooding. The card gives them a bridge. Fade cards over 4–8 weeks as the verbal replacement becomes reliable.
Can I teach multiple replacement behaviors at once?
Generally, no. Focus on the most frequent, most impairing behavior first. Teach one replacement behavior to 70–80% independence before introducing a second. Exception: if the child has multiple functions, one replacement per function may be needed simultaneously — but this requires BCBA guidance.
This all makes sense but I feel overwhelmed. Where do I start?
Start with one. One behavior. One replacement. One material. Identify: What behavior happens most frequently? What is the child getting from it? What is the simplest possible replacement that serves the same function? Teach that one for 3–4 weeks before adding anything else. Call 9100 181 181 — our team will walk you through your child's #1 priority in a single free call.
